body:
> (re: overstatements of "elite" controllers)
> Author: Pyro <Valderrey@email.msn.com>
> I am glad you brought this up.  I believe we are influenced greatly
> by both environment and culture, but truths regarding the influence
> of genes on our outcome, in terms of extent, has been greatly
> suppressed.  When I suggested that genes might play a role on the
> outcome of our political affiliations, it was a statement based on
> intuition.  It would be very difficult to prove conclusively that
> some gene or set of genes makes one a "conservative" or "liberal", a
> "fascist" or "Marxist", etc.  Again, I believe that genes _may_ serve
> as one of many influences to the outcome of one's political
> affiliation.

    Well, were those "truths" being suppressed here?  Now that we
  have both perspectives "in balance" where can we go from here?


> Another point I would like to bring up is that minority groups which
> are more passionate about their beliefs can often get ahold of a
> disproportionate amount of power, through sheer will.  So, you can
> just imagine how effective propaganda can be if it can stimulate the
> more passionate types.

    Was the goal to make propaganda more effective or less effective?


> (re: origins of the notions of "evil" & "sin")
>> So now you've cavitated to my point: that indeed it -was- your
>> "overstatement" to suggest that notions of "evil" & "sin" existed
>> only on account of propagation from the "politically correct elites."

> This subtopic doesn't seem to be going anywhere.  I never said it was
> only PC'ers who are sanctimonious, and that notions of "good" and
> "evil" are spread just by "PC elites." I just pointed out that many
> PC'ers go around smearing people because they have different
> viewpoints, and carry a "holier than thou" attitude.  I believe you
> misconstrued what I said, which is nothing new.

    There's a method to my madness as follows:  you're suggesting now
  that in addition to having a "presumption" or "perception" of being
  "automatically right" that (an additional characterization) "PC'ers"
  are sanctimonious with "'holier than thou' attitudes."  It's very
  important to nail down the semantics of what you propose to say,
  because that's not too far from locating similar attitudes on the
  part of those who -critique- the "PC'ers" and/or "Jews" -- as you
  have done on this newsgroup.  As with Orwell's _Animal_Farm_ when
  I see the same tactics employed by both human capitalists and pigs
  then I can't very well distinguish the two anymore.  Later on herein
  I will be presenting a diagram with _relative_scaling_ for "degrees"
  of the "PC-attribute" you might wish to measure, so that if one may
  claim "higher-PC" over the "PC'ers" then one can play one-upmanship
  on the "holier than thou" attitude, thus becoming even more like an
  "enemy" one hates.  As for those who "smear" we have ample evidence
  from -you- of racist (anti-semitic) smearing, and I don't see how
  you can avoid the charge of being sanctimonious, "holier than them,"
  or "automatically right" (you appear to be without self-criticism),
  and in bed with those you claim are your "PC" enemies.

    If I've misconstrued, please feel free to straighten out what seems
  to be the major disconnect and discrepancy from the part of "pyro."


> (re: harassment of J. Philippe Rushton)
> Professor Rushton had always received excellent reviews from his
> superiors at the school until he drew controversy.  Once again,
> nice try.

    Prof. Rushton's research seemed to indicate that large brain-size
  implied small penis-size, and vice-versa, that large penis-size
  was highly correlated with small brain-size.  Are you claiming that
  "scientific results" of that type should -not- be controversial?
  Some professors are famous for stirring up "harassment" in order to
  popularize their findings.


> I think firing, or harassing, professors because they hold unpopular
> views, or teach unpopular _facts_, doesn't bode well for nations
> claiming to be democratic.

     At least in a free democracy we can hear of the news, because
   many other systems of government would have no publicity at all.
   There's the major difference in a nutshell.


>> Regarding Christopher Brand: this guy was mixing up race theory
>> with pedophila as if there is some connection that we're missing.

> Um, no.  He got into two seperate controversies, one of which was
> used as a pretext to get rid of him for his unpopular views over the
> other, unrelated issue.

> The first controversy began as he openly asserted that the races
> differ in intelligence, among other things, obviously.  The second
> controversy began when he asserted that psychological studies have
> shown that children who are of above-average intelligence who have
> sex with adults, in which the child is willing to engage in the act,
> do not end up with psychological conflicts when they get older,
> generally.  That's all he said.  While it did not go well with the
> Puritanical cretins in the UK, it was scientifically accurate.

    If there were "controversies" then there's some legitimate dispute
  as to alleged "science" and "accuracy."  How did (some) psychologists
  determine that there were no "conflicts" afterwards?  Even preventive
  medicine has difficulty resolving longitudinal studies.  It's much
  more difficult to define "health" than "disease" and there are still
  unresolved issues even for definitions of "mental disease" much less
  claiming to know what is "mental health."  Furthermore, an absense
  of "psychological conflicts" does not imply no impairment to mental
  health functioning.  Social taboos are not aribtrary but were also
  components of an evolving picture of human existence, and cannot be
  summarily dismissed.  We still haven't solved problems defining IQ,
  particularly if IQ is measured according to "fit" in a dysfunctional
  "industrial-technological system" causing planetary despoilation.
  So, in what sense do we know what is "above-average intelligence" if
  we haven't determined what are the genuine contributory factors for
  (natural) intelligence?

    I don't think pedophilia is defensible, even if there were "no
  detectable psychological conflicts" (rationalization par excellance)
  because these are not the sole criterion for determining whether the
  subversion and seduction of young people is deleterious to their life
  functioning.  Meeting the psychological minimum is not the measure of
  all things.  A question is not whether pedophilia impaired individuals
  below the minimal criteria for functioning, but whether possibilities
  for excellence above and beyond "minimal" standards were impaired to
  any degree whatsoever.  Once again a most vivid and horrific example
  of logical fallacy within the nut-house called pop-psychology.

                ( Matthew 18:6, Mark 9:42, Luke 17:2 )


> (re: Kaczynski quote)
>> |  "Propaganda for example is used for many good purposes,   |
>> |   such as discouraging child abuse or race hatred. [14]"   |
>
> Sounds to me like something Dick Armey or George Bush Jr. would say.

     Your point being .... ?


>(re: Ms. Gottfredson and $177,541 in Pioneer Funds)
> ... I think standards are extremely important, especially in
> universities.  However, there is a critical distinction between
> firing a professor because he is a non-productive louse and firing
> one merely because he holds unpopular views, even though he does his
> job well.  You are showing the arrogance PC'ers hold, which I have
> been talking about.  Who are you, or the chancellor of a university,
> or anyone else, to tell a professor he should resign because his work
> is "improper", even as the professor has engaged in groundbreaking
> work and has contributed to an area of science to which few or none
> can match?

    Nobody stopped Ms. Gottfredson from continuing her research, as is
  the perogative of any professional desirous of scientific integrity.
  Nobody told Ms. Gottfredson that she should resign on account of her
  "work."  So far, the issue presented to her concerned a University
  Policy prohibitive of the receipt of funds from a "special-interest
  group" identified as racist.  The chancellor, the board of regents,
  the president:  all are beholden to outside factors stemming from a
  state legislature, the taxpayers, obligation to alumni, the business
  community.  Any component of the process is subject to review and/or
  replacement if deemed unsuitable.  Ms. Gottfredson could have pursued
  litigation yet decided against it, if Pioneer Funds were so all-fired
  critically important.  I'll ask you again:  what were the conclusions
  you expected Ms. Gottfredson to reach, and what possible impact would
  any potential conclusion have upon shaping social policy concerns?


> (re: race differences and genes)
>> The "conclusive proof" is available by creating opportunities and
>> allowing them to succeed or to wash-out in higher-education courses.

> This sounds nice, but you need to be specific as to what you mean by
> "opportunities".  I mean, I just applied for a job and because I am
> "Hispanic" (by the absurd technicality of subconscious racist
> Anglo-Saxon do-gooders) I am fairly confident I will get the job, and
> be automatically given more points on the cognitive exam than my
> white counterparts (even though I would have scored higher than
> virtually all of them without the help).  Yes, sounds like an
> oppressive system.

     I agree that affirmative action hiring quotas shouldn't work by
   adding points to a "cognitive exam" (if that's really the case).
   There's no advantage in disguising affirmative action as something
   else.  In fact those who might oppose affirmative action, could on
   principle be those the programs were designed to benefit.  The fact
   that opposition to affirmative action does not stem from those who
   "benefit to excess" indicates their degree of insecurity and greed.
   I would prefer my resume to reflect hiring by merit rather than by
   affirmative action.  If you don't sense "oppression" then perhaps
   you're not sufficiently challenged.  May I recommend the library?


>> It seems to me, however, that once deciding opportunities should not
>> be allowed (on pretext of "genetic" impairment applied to classes of
>> individuals rather than to the individuals themselves) then one would
>> effectively -sabotage- a viability of any further "conclusive proof"
>> in the evaluative context of those higher-education courses.

> _Non-sequitur_.  Ms. Gottfredson, and other race-realist academics,
> are not out to keep certain groups from having the same opportunities
> as everyone else.  They are out to find and expose the truth; they
> are trying to be objective.

    If they're just diddling each other with sociological narcissism
  then that's yet another argument there upon academic irrelevance.
  "Objectivity" is not the singular goal of science, by the way, since
  we are also interested in obtaining data that provides some answers
  to the question of how to chart social policy.  If Ms. Gottfredson's
  work isn't going to inform us about social policies, then where was
  the "statement of purpose" motivating her studies?  A _sequitur_ to
  my fundamental argument still remains even if it's not going to apply
  (as -you- claim) to Ms. Gottfredson, or "other race-realist academics"
  (though there are, undoubtedly, many "race-realist academics" who are
  acutely attuned to potential social policy effects of their research).
  Thereby a "flip side" of that issue presented itself when you asked:


(re: "academic freedom" and/or that fundamental question)
> How are we to establish effective social policies if we don't know
> why things are the way they are?

    ... yielding a "chicken-and-egg" dilemma.  To unravel it, let's ask
  first if the "role of science" can possibly provide answer(s) to "why
  things are the way they are" or -- more pragmatically -- whether we
  may expect of science only a function of fulfilling "theory creation"
  and provisional explanation of data.  A "science" claiming to offer
  answers to fundamental "why" questions runs the risk of not anymore
  being science but becoming "scientism," i.e. science arrogating an
  expertise over regions of inquiry formerly assigned to religion. TK's
  view seems to be that religion won't be replaced by science -- and he
  seems to state that religion most definitely should not be replaced
  by those aspects of "science" which are High-Technology -- so one
  could adopt, or share, TK's views wholesale or dispute them outright
  or in part, which seems to be the point of focus for this newsgroup.


> (re: is TK a closet Nazi?)
>> If we're to avoid media bias it might be worthwhile to move toward
>> the direction of being like a court room.

> You have convinced me that TK has never contacted any Nazi
> organization. :-)

    This admission seems to be rather important, since Ross Getman had
  stated his reason for abandoning a.f.u. was due to -your- insistence
  on conflating TK with Nazism, and now you owe an apology to Ross for
  mischaracterizing his statements.


> However.. as you pointed out, media bias against Kaczynski was shown
> by their clumping him with neo-Nazis.  This reinforces my view of how
> people use the "Nazi" label to smear, especially those who are
> clearly _not_ Nazis, who happen to be "undesirable", or have
> undesirable opinions.

    I'm in agreement that "media bias" occurs through miscategorization
  via "clumping" since a presumption on the part of mass-media is that
  "news consumers" have neither an interest nor the sophistication for
  factual details which lead to differentiation of cases, distinguishing
  TK from other unrelated incidents, even as we all recognize generally
  that "justice" initially requires case-by-case treatment for meeting
  the requirements of due process and equal protection.  Often as not,
  the news reporters themselves lack the interest and sophistication to
  provide accurate and thorough coverage, and in more than a few cases
  the news reporters are simply corporate shills, or puppets of statist
  agenda.  Debates about "journalistic ethics" are largely unresolved
  and ongoing, and are usually unhelpful when discussed after the fact,
  which unfortunately is also most usually the situation.  With regards
  to TK, a feature of TK's peculiar violent methods must have prejudiced
  mass-media against the possibility of a reasoned forum for carefully
  detached and insightful remarks.  "Who people are" and "what they do"
  are also too often conflated by an overtly simplistic/reductionistic
  mass-media.  Mass-media is itself merely an aggregate of individual
  contributions, and each of those individuals is operating from some
  simplistic/reductionistic "world-view" or perspective on things, so
  the sum of parts might be nothing more than "more parts" and never
  attain wholism.  One doesn't locate wholism simply by summation since
  there might be many different approaches to obtaining an addition of
  many highly-unrelated discrete components.  Philosophical wholism
  usually needs to proceed from a notion of completedness or closure,
  as with drawing a circular (or spherical) boundary.  Mass-media seems
  unwilling to entertain that idea, opting instead for their peculiar
  brand of asinine chaos.  The marketplace is an inferior as judge of
  cultural forms, however, servile journalists seem to take their cues
  primarily from marketplace fashions rather than depicting long-range
  perspectives from which activity in the present-tense can better be
  coordinated.  There is resistance to forms of wholism that are drawn
  too narrowly, or without sufficient dimensionality, so understanding
  of higher-dimensional properties (i.e. packing, density, tangency,
  codings, lattices, algebraic geometry, etc.) may be the prerequisite
  for constructed wholism with sufficiently comprehensive boundaries.
  Again, most journalists are woefully undereducated in mathematics.

    If mass-media was labelled "PC" and if this forum can attain a
  level of non-spin objectivity unavailable in mass-media, then perhaps
  it's also appropriate to demolish the "PC" notion.  It's paradoxical
  to assert positions "more correct" than "political correctness" since
  that notion introduces fluidity and redefinition of terms.  Rather
  than polarizing perspectives and propositional statements into two
  boxes labelled "PC" & "non-PC" it may be helpful to consider complex
  spectra of views running, more or less, along two intersecting axis:


                                   true                e
                            c        |
            a                        |       d
                  b                  |
                                     |                   f
                                     |
     politically incorrect ----------+---------- politically correct
                                     |
           j          l              |     g                 i
                                m    |
                 k                   |               h
                                     |
                                   false


  with letters (a...m) identifying a number of sample "positions" on the
  chart.  I'm hoping we can work from this diagram, or one similar, and
  if you'd like to propose an alternative then by all means do so.  It's
  essential to disentangle any -necessary- association of "PC"/"non-PC"
  with notions of "true"/"false" (or other variations: "The True", etc).
  If there's a position qualifying as both "non-PC" and "true" then it
  can be identified by marking its location on the diagram somewhere
  nearby to letter "a." Positions in general, however, might not all be
  aligned along a diagonal running from "a" through "h" since we might
  also encounter perspectives and views which run along a diagonal from
  "k" through "e" and so all over the map of this diagram. A fundamental
  identifier distinguishing these two axis may be provided by contextual
  comparison:  the "correct" or "incorrect" according to politics was
  determined by socio-political alignments, something akin to majority
  will.  A "true" or "false" axis boils down to insertion of individual
  assessment, evaluation, review, and/or initiation of perspectives that
  may or may not be in accord with the majority.  The diagram itself can
  be subjective when two individuals disagree over phenomena along the
  horizontal axis (such as differences among polling results), and will
  be subjective when two individuals encounter variances along vertical
  axis estimations of the relative "truth" or "falsity" of some given
  propositional construct.  The relative "degree of subjectivity" to
  such diagrams is simply accumulated "measure of statistical variance"
  among positions (a...m) and (a'...m') -- unprimed and primed diagrams
  -- obtained by summing:

   ___
   \
     \   A*A'*(a - a')^2 + B*B'*(b - b')^2 + C*C'*(c - c')^2 ...
     /
   /___


  for each of the diagrammed positions (a...m) and (a'...m') with their
  corresponding relative weight factors (A...M) and (A'...M') assigned
  to each of the positions in the diagrams, since not all individuals
  will necessarily regard a given set of propositional statements, or
  positions, or perspectives, or views, as equally weighted.  They might
  want to introduce measures of _relative_importance_ to variations from
  their precise locations, as placed within their respective bi-axial
  correspondence frames.

    Perhaps we can avoid the clumping of "media bias" once developing
  an understanding for categorical taxonomy of perspectives, according
  to the generalized characterization for orthogonal axis utilized for
  representing the relationship between an individual and society, and
  then by comparison, among individuals and societies.  Elsewhere on
  this newsgroup you have criticized (say) "Jews" for being "too PC,"
  however if they are to sustain -your- criticism, then in that context
  -you- wish to propose they are -not- "PC" -- or are "non-PC" -- and
  so we would have the confusion of contexts and thereby an intrinsic
  paradox to what appears to be untenable:  your anti-semitism asks an
  audience to accept that some group could be "non-PC" because they are
  "too PC" so you'd need to establish the precise manner in which that
  diagram has "wrap around" -- of which there are several varieties --
  providing some justification for why you've chosen a particular model.
  If, instead you wish -not- to communicate by clarifying those points
  sufficiently, then the  'net.consequence'  of your "theorization"
  runs the risk of becoming little more than a fart in the wind.  Also,
  if hyperspace "wrap around" (such as the video-game *Asteroids*) is
  your 'solution' or explanation of why a "PC" group could be relabelled
  as "non-PC" then you'd also need to describe just what is implied by
  an ordering relation on horizontal and/or vertical axis.

    Furthermore, since this is the newsgroup  "alt.fan.unabomber"  any
  reference to "Nazis" should be related in some manner to the topic of
  discussion, as to how and what TK advocated, and whether or not there
  is agreement/disagreement, and perhaps why or why not, etc.  Had TK
  been targeting "semites" or were such affiliations incidental?  The
  three contexts for "nazi" in his Manifesto occur in:

      (a) par.83 -- how the "power process" for identifying with mass
    movements is "exploited by the fascists, nazis, and communists."

      (b) par.161 -- how behavioral psychology is also an instance of
    "technical advance" for "controlling human beings" though "not ...
    impressively successful."  TK says there are "growing numbers ...
    who ... are rebels against the system:  welfare leaches, youth
    gangs cultists, satanists, nazis, radical environmentalists,
    militiamen, etc."  Interpreting this paragraph is difficult, since
    TK is diagnosing ills of the system as inherent pathologies to the
    "industrial-technological system."  Evidence of the pathology is
    being provided by increasing numbers of rebels.  Then, among the
    itemized groups listed, TK includes "radical environmentalists"
    as if there should be some kind of guilt-by-association.  This is
    a confusing passage since "radical environmentalism" might be a
    popular term with some personality types, so why is TK associating
    them with leaches, cultists, gangs, satanists, nazis, militiamen?
    There is a double-take "irony" involved in that passage:  TK is
    (1) saying that "radical environmentalists" (however commendable)
    are also themselves evidence of pathology in a crumbling ITS.
    However para.161 was discussing how "to integrate these techniques
    into a functioning social system" via "educational psychology" and
    some possible "advances relating to human behavior."  So TK is also
    (2) sounding a call to those who might be "leaches, cultists, gangs,
    satanists, nazis, militiamen, etc." to consider taking up a banner
    of "radical environmentalism."  The placement of "environmentalism"
    among those other groups was woefully incongruous, yet we might
    take into account that TK was/is a mathematician, perhaps with some
    sense of humor:  "The teachers are too busy taking knives and guns
    away from the kids to subject them to the latest techniques for
    making them into computer nerds."  TK will detail those "latest
    techniques" in the final sentence of para.161, slipping in a bit of
    subliminal programming.  TK was a professor, and very likely still
    remains a 'teacher' actively engaged in "taking knives and guns
    away from kids" also through "radical environmentalism" -- a third
    irony -- perhaps an exquisite interpretation available only for
    those inclined by higher mathematics, which is neither the same as
    high technology nor scientism.

      (c) par.222:  The irony agains run thick.  TK invokes a reference
    to "True Believers" and then trots out a proposition concerning an
    assertion of -attribute- for those "True Believers" (as if we really
    can be all that knowledgeable about a phenomenon poorly understood).
    How can anyone be certain that "not all True Believers are of the
    same psychological type as leftists" ? The only source for possible
    certainty seems to follow from the general condition that it's not
    unsafe to assume Venn diagrams for concept apprehension. TK follows
    with:  "Presumably" (sic!) "a truebelieving nazi, for instance is
    very different psychologically from a truebelieving leftist."  Well
    of course, wasn't that Hitler's point-of-contention against the
    German communist party?  Why, then, is TK saying "presumably" ?  It
    is an _obvious_point_ not requiring presumption!  Again, TK asks
    those who would be "nazis" to consider "psychological differences."
    Eric Hoffer's books were among many titles directed at analyzing the
    causes of Nazi Germany.  The phenomenon of a "True Believer" was
    being identified as a -problem- within the human condition, so the
    the book _The_True_Believer_ was designed to be an anti-nazi tract.
    Like Hoffer, TK pokes fun at "leftists" but considers them far less
    dangerous to sustainable civilization than nazis.  "This presents a
    problem with which we must admit we don't know how to deal."  (This
    is a statement of -perplexity- !) "We aren't sure how to harness the
    energies of the True Believer to a revolution against technology."
    (Because such harnessing would itself be a behavioral technology.)
    Then TK sets about "harnessing" them anyway:  "...no True Believer
    will make a safe recruit to the revolution unless his commitment is
    exclusively to the destruction of technology..." because TK advances
    the "definition via negative" attempting to 'hook' the reader into
    accepting a particular interpretation of what TK thinks the person
    identified as "True Believer" should be.  In order to understand
    what paragraph #222 is about some investigation needs to proceed on
    the semantic merits of what the word "technology" means, and why TK
    thinks it needs destruction in order to save the human species.

   There was -no- invocation of "race agenda" or "pedophilia" involved
  in TK's narrowly stated goal of exclusive commitment.  In what way,
  then do people like J.Phillip Rushton, Chris Brand, or Ms.Gottfredson
  bear upon TK's description of his revolution?  Either relevance, or
  that "True Believer" will -not- make a "safe recruit."   Q.E.D.


>> Double-negatives don't necessarily render a positive, and also
>> one might dislike certain political groups because they are -not-
>> sufficiently radical, or simply because they do not share common
>> interests (i.e. were "hippie protestors" conversant in "boundary
>> functions" and/or general mathematical topics?).

> Oh, c'mon.  The liberal professors egged on the radicals of the '60s.
> It seems to me you are doing some rationalizing -- and you are good
> at it (I don't mean this in an offensive way).

    Not all liberal professors were throwing eggs, so who is actually
  doing the "rationalizing" here?  Rational thinking is distinct from
  rationalizing, because rational thinking is open-minded while the
  device of rationalizing is employed to justify a closed-mind.  The
  closed mind works by -presuming- a conclusion and then attempting to
  fit facts into some peculiar twist.  You would suggest for us that
  "any professor who did not egg on the '60s radicals" could not be a
  liberal, which is the sort of untenable hypothesis that could proceed
  only from a closed-mind.  Your example (above) provided illustration
  of not only "rationalization" but also "rationalization with covert
  projection" (claiming -others- are that cause of "rationlization").


>> The closest I can find, from the Manifesto, is TK's affiliation
>> with anarchism, which is completely at variance to the corporate
>> right-wing, or to platitudinous National Socialism, since TK used
>> the phrase "our particular brand of anarchism" in footnote #34.
>> Elsewhere TK is extraordinarily verbose on how both "right-wing"
>> and "left-wing" desire High-Technology as a means of controlling
>> their organizations and national electorate. The bottom line is
>> that TK cannot be categorized even remotely near the right-wing.

> Platitudinous National Socialism? A platitude is an over-used word or
> phrase.  While the Nazis undoubtedly had many platitudes in their
> day, their slogans are fairly obscure to the general public today.
> National Socialists are merely at one extreme, and the PC'ers are
> diametrically at the opposing end.

    We have a new (complex) model, now, where you can try a recasting
  of your political chart.  There are -many- instances of what may
  constitute a "fringe" (extremist) group.  When speaking of "opposite"
  one might refer to "inverting about X-axis" or "inverting about Y"
  or "inverting about both" or introducing a new/previously unanalyzed
  dimension.  It is quite obviously a mistake to claim that one group
  might have some (conspiratorial) connection to another simply because
  both can be considered extremist.  As for platitudes, the literature
  of _Mein_Kampf_ has been analyzed for its "plethora of proverbs" --
  of which Hitler was well versed -- and most acknowledge Hitler as a
  master deceptionist with propaganda.  The fundamental question still
  remains:  why were so many deceived by Hitler's insane program which
  led Germany into yet another plan of self-destruction?  His war was
  (paradoxically) the destruction of Germany and its people, completely
  -unlike- an agenda to "destroy technology" which is non-specific, has
  no nationalism, is not directed at any racial group, considers the
  longest-range viewpoint possible, does not involve political activity,
  is not interested in leading large numbers of "true believing" sheep,
  is uninterested by economic self-aggrandizement or conquests of more
  territory.  No resemblance between propaganda and anti-propaganda.


> (re: "commies" and McCarthyism)
>> So smear McCarthyism could be justified upon organizations
>> advocating violence against the state?

> Where would we draw the line? The Communists in the '50s were
> perceived as very threatening to the state; we were in a Cold War.
> Communists were stealing nuclear secrets and handing them to the
> Soviets.  I hate the current state of affairs, and hope the system
> collapses.  But I don't advocate violence against the system, or to
> anyone in particular.  I just hope it self-destructs -- and it may,
> who knows. . .

> Modern day fascists seem to hold views more in line with what the
> Founding Fathers believed.  The Founding Fathers were far more racist
> than most realize.  (By Founding Fathers I mean American
> Revolutionaries, in case you are not American).

    Well yes, the embarassment of a Civil War is the legacy of -their-
  original Constitution, though a few had the prescience to speculate
  upon likelihood of modification to a living document.  One might also
  instead say that the War of Independence had much to do with forcing
